## Rubin causal model

The Rubin causal model (RCM), also known as the Neyman-Rubin causal model, is an approach to the statistical analysis of cause and effect based on the framework of potential outcomes, named after Donald Rubin. 

Let $T$ be the label of treatment and let $C$ be the label of control. Let $Y_{T,i}$ be the “potential” outcome for subject $i$ in the treatment condition and $Y_{C,i}$ be the potential outcome for subject $i$ in the control condition. 
$$
\begin{align}
y_i = T_i Y_{T,i} + (1-T_i) Y_{C,i}
\label{eq:rubin_model}
\end{align}
$$
In the Neyman-Rubin model, potential outcomes are fixed and the only source of randomness is $T_i$. This model is **nonparametric** because
it does not depend on the potential outcome distributions.  

The averaged difference between the two potential outcomes over all subjects is of interest by researchers, which is termed as the average treatment effect (ATE),
$$
\begin{align}
    \tau
    = \bar{Y}_{T} - \bar{Y}_{C}
    = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{T,i} - Y_{C,i}) .
\end{align}
$$
Denote by $\tau_i=Y_{T,i} - Y_{C,i}$ the individual treatment effect (ITE) of the $i$th subject. 

Note that the ATE parameter $\tau$ cannot be calculated directly because potential outcomes for each subject cannot be observed in both the treatment and control conditions. 



### Randomized treatment assignment

The biggest difference between RCT data and a observational data lies the assignment of treatment or control condition to subjections/samples. They considered RCTs with a single treatment and control group. It is assumed that the missing data process for study outcomes is independent of treatment status. 

In the following we assume that the experiments are conducted with randomized treatment. This randomization ensures that treatment assignment is not influenced by any potential confounding factors. 

Assume that we have $n$ subjects which are assigned to treatment or control condition. The sample contains $np$ treatments and $n(1-\rho)$ controls where $\rho$ is the sampling rate to the treatment group. 

### Method 1: Difference between treated and controlled

The simplest method to estimate ATE is using the difference between the treated group and the controlled group, 
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}
= \frac{1}{np} \sum_{i\in\{i \mid T_i = 1\}} y_i - \frac{1}{n(1-p)} \sum_{i\in\{i \mid T_i = 0\}} y_i .
\end{align}
$$
### Method 1’: Simple regression

Let $T$ be the treatment status indicator. $T$ is a $0-1$ random variable,  $T=1$ for treatment and $T=0$ for control. To investigate the regression estimator, a structural regression model implied by the Neyman model can be constructed by re-writing $\eqref{eq:rubin_model}$ as 
$$
\begin{align}
y_i = \tau (T_i - \rho) + \mu + e_i
\label{eq:statists_model_1}
\end{align}
$$
where $y_i$ is the $i$th observed outcome; $T_i$ is the $i$th treatment status; $\mu$ is the average outcome; $e_i$ is the “error” term. Specifically, 
$$
\begin{align}
	\begin{aligned}[b]
		\mu 	& = \rho \bar{Y}_T + (1-\rho) \bar{Y}_C , \\
		e_i 	& = \Delta_i + \nu_i (T_i - \rho), \\
		\Delta_i& = \rho(Y_{T,i} - \bar{Y}_T) + (1-\rho) (Y_{C,i} - \bar{Y}_C), \\
		\nu_i	& = (Y_{T,i} - \bar{Y}_T) - (Y_{C,i} - \bar{Y}_C), 
	\end{aligned}
	\label{eq:terms_in_model}
\end{align}
$$

where $\Delta_i$ is the weighted deviation of the $i$th individual potential outcome from the corresponding average outcome,  $\nu_i$ is the deviation of the  $i$th individual treatment effect (ITE) from the corresponding average treatment effect. Schochet (2010) [^1] pointed out that the model $\eqref{eq:statists_model_1}$ does not satisfy Gaussian-Markov assumption of the OLS model. 

The simple regression estimator $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ is obtained by running a regression of $Y$ against $T$ in model $\eqref{eq:statists_model_1}$, i.e.,  
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\tau}^{(2)} = \frac{\sum\left(T_{i}-\bar{T}\right)\left(y_{i}-\bar{y}\right)}{\sum\left(T_{i}-\bar{T}\right)^{2}} = \frac{\sum\left(T_{i}-\rho\right)y_{i}}{n\rho(1-\rho)}. 
\end{align}
$$
​	1. Equivalence

$$
\begin{align}
    \begin{aligned}[b]
    \widehat{\tau}^{(1)}
    &= \frac{\sum T_{i} Y_{i}}{\sum T_{i}}-\frac{\sum\left(1-T_{i}\right) Y_{i}}{\sum\left(1-T_{i}\right)} \\
    &= \frac{n^{-1}\sum T_{i} Y_{i}}{\rho} - \frac{n^{-1}\sum Y_{i} - n^{-1}\sum T_{i} Y_{i} }{1-\rho} \\
    &= \frac{n^{-1}\sum T_{i} Y_{i} - (n^{-1}\sum T_{i}) (n^{-1}\sum Y_{i})}{\rho(1-\rho)} \\
    &= \frac{\operatorname{cov}(T, Y)}{\operatorname{var}(T)} 
    = \widehat{\tau}^{(2)}
    \end{aligned}
\end{align}
$$

​	2.  Unbiasedness

The randomization of treatment condition ensures that $\frac{\sum T_{i} Y_{i}}{n\rho}$ is an unbiased estimator of $Y_T$ and that $\frac{\sum (1-T_{i}) Y_{i}}{n(1-\rho)}$ is an unbiased estimator of $Y_C$. Thus, $\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\tau=Y_T-T_C$. 

​	3. Variance of estimators

In order to analyze the variance of the estimator, we need to substitute the model in $\eqref{eq:statists_model_1}$ into the estimator $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$,
$$
\begin{align}
    \widehat{\tau}^{(2)} 
    = \frac{\sum\left(T_{i}-\rho\right)y_{i}}{n\rho(1-\rho)}
    = \tau + \frac{\sum\left(T_{i}-\rho\right)e_{i}}{n\rho(1-\rho)}. 
\end{align}
$$

Substituting for $e_i$ using $\eqref{eq:terms_in_model}$ yields: 
$$
\begin{align}
    \widehat{\tau}^{(2)} - \tau 
    = \frac{\sum\left(T_{i}-\rho\right)e_{i}}{n\rho(1-\rho)} 
    = \frac{\sum \left[ \left\{(1-\rho)(Y_{T,i} - \bar{Y}_T) + \rho(Y_{C,i} - \bar{Y}_C)\right\}T_{i} \right]}{n\rho(1-\rho)} 
    :=  \frac{\sum \ell_i T_{i}}{n\rho(1-\rho)}
    \label{eq:bias_1}
\end{align}
$$
where $\ell_i=(1-\rho)(Y_{T,i} - \bar{Y}_T) + \rho(Y_{C,i} - \bar{Y}_C)$.  According to $\eqref{eq:bias_1}$, $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ is unbiased because $\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\tau}^{(2)} - \tau) = 0$. Further, we have the variance of $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$,
$$
\begin{align}
	\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}) 
	= \frac{\mathrm{Var} \left( \sum \ell_i T_{i} \right)}{n^2\rho^2(1-\rho)^2}
	= \frac{\sum_i \mathrm{Var} \left(  \ell_i T_{i} \right) + \sum_{j \neq k}\ell_j \ell_k \mathrm{Cov}(T_j, T_k)}{n^2\rho^2(1-\rho)^2}
	= \dots
	= \frac{S_T^2}{np} + \frac{S_C^2}{n(1-p)} - \frac{S_{\tau}^2}{n} ,
\end{align}
$$
where $S_T^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{T,i} - \bar{Y}_{T})^2$ is the variance of the potential treatment outcomes across the $n$ subjects, $S_C^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{C,i} - \bar{Y}_{C})^2$ is the variance of the potential control outcomes, and $S_{\tau}^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\nu_i^2$ is the variance of the individual-level treatment effects. 

4. Asymptotic normality

According to $\eqref{eq:bias_1}$, 
$$
\begin{align}
\sqrt{n}\rho(1-\rho) (\widehat{\tau}^{(2)} - \tau ) = \frac{\sum (T_i-\rho)e_i}{\sqrt{n}} ,
\end{align}
$$
the asymptotic normality of $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ is obtained using CLT for finite populations under some regular condition on $\rho$, $Y_{T,i}$, $Y_{C,i}$ and $\nu_i$. Assume that,  as n increases to infinity, 
$$
\begin{align}
	S_{T}^{2} \rightarrow \bar{S}_{T}^{2}, 
	\quad S_{C}^{2} \rightarrow \bar{S}_{C}^{2}, 
	\quad S_{\tau}^{2} \rightarrow \bar{S}_{\tau}^{2}, 
\end{align}
$$
where where $\bar{S}_{T}^{2}$, $\bar{S}_{C}^{2}$, $\bar{S}_{\tau}^{2}$ are fixed, nonnegative, real numbers. Then, the asymptotic variance is 
$$
\begin{align}
    \mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}) 
    = \frac{\bar{S}_T^2}{np} + \frac{\bar{S}_C^2}{n(1-p)} - \frac{\bar{S}_{\tau}^2}{n} . 
\end{align}
$$


## Covariates adjustment average treatment effect

Schochet (2010) analyzed the estimation of average treatment effect (ATE) under an randomized controlled trials (RCTs). They focused on the use of regression models to increase the precision of estimator of ATE. Let’s consider a more specific regression model than $\eqref{eq:statists_model_1}$, 

$$
\begin{align}
	y = \tau (T-\rho) + X \beta + e
	\label{eq:statists_model_2}
\end{align}
$$
where $y$ is an $n\times1$ vector of observed outcomes; $T$ is an $n\times1$ vector; $X$ is an $n\times p$ real-valued matrix with its first column being $1$s. The model in $\eqref{eq:statists_model_2}$ means that the average outcome $\mu$ in $\eqref{eq:statists_model_1}$ is a linear combination of $X$. Note that, linear structure in $$\eqref{eq:statists_model_2}$$ is a special case. 

### Method 3: Covariates-adjustment regression

We use the covariates $X$ to regress $y$ which could help to improve the estimate of ATE. The least square estimator for $\tau$ is as follows:
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\tau}^{(3)} = \{ \tilde{T}^\prime (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X) \tilde{T} \}^{-1} \tilde{T}^\prime (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X) y .
\label{eq:lse}
\end{align}
$$
where $\tilde{T}=T-\rho\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times1}$ and  $\mathbf{P}_X \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is the projection matrix of $X$. We can find that $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ is a special case of $\eqref{eq:lse}$ where $X$ only have a column of $1$s. The term $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X)$ is a weight matrix which makes sure that the projection from $y$ to the column space of $T$ eliminates the impact of column space of $X$, such that $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$ is the estimate of linear impact of $T$ on $y$, i.e., ATE. 事实上, 由于实验的随机性, T 与 X 是独立的, 所以, 投影矩阵是无效的??. 

Schochet (2010) proved that, if
$$
\begin{align}
    \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \tilde{\mathbf{X}}}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}, 
    \quad \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \Delta}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}, 
    \quad \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \nu}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \nu}, 
\end{align}
$$
as $n$ goes to infinity. Then, we have,
$$
\begin{align}
    \mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}\right)
    =
    \left(\frac{\bar{S}_{T}^{2}}{n p}+\frac{\bar{S}_{C}^{2}}{n(1-p)}
    - \frac{\bar{S}_{\tau}^{2}}{n}\right)-\frac{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}^{\prime} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}}{n p(1-p)}
    -2(1-2 p) \frac{\mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X \nu}}^{\prime} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}^{-1} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}}{n p(1-p)} . 
\end{align}
$$

Under some scenarios, the third term is positive or third term is smaller than the second term, $\mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}\right)$ is smaller than $\mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}\right)$. 

### Simulation

Now, let's consider a simple numerical experiment to intuitively observe the above two regression estimators $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ and $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$ to prove that considering covariate $X$ can indeed reduce variance. 

We generate $50$ samples by $y= T + X + 0.5e$ where $20$ samples are treated and $30$ samples are controlled, $X$ and $e$ are from i.i.d. standard normal distribution. 

Let’s look at $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$, it separates samples by treatment status and estimates the average outcome in each group. Then, the ATE estimate is the difference of the outcomes. As shown in the following figure. 

<img src="D:\OneDrive\Documents\Writings\assets\2021-04-29-0001.png" alt="2021-04-29-0002" style="zoom:38%;" />

It shows that the two sets of samples are chaotically distributed on the line $T=0$ and $T=1$, and it is difficult to distinguish the difference between the two sets of data. The variance of outcomes in each group is large, and the mean value could be unstable. Actually, $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}=0.44$ is far away from the true value $\tau=1$. 

Next, let’s check what’s going on when $X$ is used in the estimation. We regress $y$ against $X$ in the two group separately. 

<img src="D:\OneDrive\Documents\Writings\assets\2021-04-29-0002.png" alt="2021-04-29-0002" style="zoom:38%;" />

The samples are arranged near the regression line with a small variance. $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}=0.81$ is closer to the true value, $\tau=1$. 

Also note that the the means of $X$s in both group are different, as the red dots shown in the figure. It could lead to the miss under-estimation or over-estimation of $\tau$. The red dots is in the regression lines. Thus $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$ is a kind of adjustment for $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$. 

但是我们任然要注意到, 在样本较大的时候, 两个估计量都会以较快的速度收敛到真值. 估计量的微小的方差可以忽略不记. 

## Model selection

Bloniarz, et, al. (2016) [^3] provided a principled way for investigators to analyze randomized experiments when the number of covariates is large. 

They re-written the estimator $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$ as 
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}
=
\left[\widehat{Y}_T - (\bar{X}_T - \bar{X})^\prime \widehat{\beta}_T \right] - \left[\widehat{Y}_C - (\bar{X}_C - \bar{X})^\prime \widehat{\beta}_C \right] . 
\end{align}
$$
When we have a large number of covariates, how to estimate $\beta$ is a problem. This is a tradeoff between bias and variance. If we use only a little covariates, the estimator may still have a big variance. If we use too many covariates, it could over-fitting and lead to a biased ATE estimator. 
Bloniarz, et, al. (2016) [^3] proposed a Lasso estimator of $\beta$s, 
$$
\begin{align}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text {Lasso,T}}
=
\underset{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\arg \min }\left[\frac{1}{2 n\rho} \sum_{i \in T}\left(y_{i}-\bar{y}_{T}-\left(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{T}\right)^\prime \boldsymbol{\beta}\right)^{2}+\lambda_{T} \sum_{j=1}^{p}\left|\beta_{j}\right|\right] ,
\end{align}
$$
and
$$
\begin{align}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text {Lasso,C}}
=
\underset{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\arg \min }\left[\frac{1}{2 n(1-\rho)} \sum_{i \in C}\left(y_{i}-\bar{y}_{C}-\left(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{C}\right)^\prime \boldsymbol{\beta}\right)^{2}+\lambda_{C} \sum_{j=1}^{p}\left|\beta_{j}\right|\right] ,
\end{align}
$$
Where the tuning parameters $\lambda_{T}$ and $\lambda_{C}$ are chosen by cross-validation (CV). 

Then, the Lasso-adjusted ATE estimator is
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\tau}_{\text {Lasso}}
=
\left[\bar{y}_{T}-\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{T}-\overline{\mathbf{x}}\right)^\prime \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{Lasso,T}}\right]
-
\left[\bar{y}_{C}-\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{C}-\overline{\mathbf{x}}\right)^\prime \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{Lasso,C}}\right] . 
\end{align}
$$
They proved the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\tau}_{\text {Lasso}}$.
